analysis.one_liner: Requires voter-verified paper ballots, post-election audits, and cybersecurity rules for federal elections, with grants to help states pay.
analysis.headline: The election-security bill drew 16 cosponsors but was referred to the Senate Rules Committee on day one and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Act would have required every federal election to use voter-verifiable paper ballots as the official record, banned voting machines from connecting to the internet, and required states to conduct statistical post-election audits that check machine counts against paper. It paired those mandates with federal grants — over $1 billion authorized across several programs — to help states replace old machines, buy accessible ballot-marking devices for voters with disabilities, and print ballots. It also imposed new duties on voting machine makers: manufacture in the US, disclose source code under an open license, and submit to federal cybersecurity testing.
analysis.who_benefits: American voters, who would get a hand-verifiable paper record behind every federal vote and audits that catch miscounts; voters with disabilities, who would get federally funded accessible ballot-marking devices; and voters with limited English or literacy, whose access would be studied and improved. State and local election offices would receive grant money to replace aging machines and harden voter registration systems.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal election to use an individual, durable, voter-verifiable paper ballot that the voter inspects before casting; the paper ballot becomes the official record and is counted by hand in any recount.
Bans voting systems from being connected to the internet or using wireless or concealed communication devices for federal elections starting in 2020.

Requires every state to conduct risk-limiting audits — statistically rigorous hand checks of machine-counted results against paper ballots — in all federal elections, with federal funding for the audits.

Authorizes large federal grants to states: $600 million plus $175 million in alternating fiscal years to replace noncompliant voting systems and harden election security, $250 million for accessible ballot-marking devices for voters with disabilities, and additional 'such sums as necessary' for ballot printing and audit costs.

Requires the National Science Foundation to fund research on making paper ballot voting usable for voters with disabilities, voters whose primary language is not English, and voters with literacy difficulties, with any resulting technology made public and non-proprietary.

Directs the Department of Homeland Security to set mandatory cybersecurity standards for voting equipment, voter registration databases, and electronic poll books, and to test and certify ballot-marking and tabulation devices at no charge, with the power to decertify systems that fail.

Requires voting systems to be manufactured in the United States and manufacturers to publicly disclose their source code under a royalty-free open license and their hardware components, so independent researchers can inspect them.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the grant programs (over $1 billion authorized, plus open-ended spending for audits and printing). State and local election offices bear compliance costs to the extent grants fall short — the bill itself provides for pro-rata cuts to state grants if appropriations are insufficient. Voting machine manufacturers bear the largest new private cost: redesigning systems around hand-marked paper, publishing proprietary source code, disclosing hardware designs, disconnecting machines, and US-only manufacturing.

drawbacks.text: The federal cost is substantial: $600 million plus $175 million in alternating fiscal years, $250 million for accessible devices, and open-ended funding for audits and ballot printing — all subject to annual appropriations, and the bill explicitly cuts state grants pro rata if Congress does not appropriate enough.

The timeline was tight: most requirements would take effect for the 2020 elections, leaving states months to replace machines and retrain poll workers; jurisdictions using older paper-trail printers got only a two-year delay to 2022, with a legal duty to offer hand-marked paper ballots and keep waits under 30 minutes in the meantime.

The bill requires hand counting of every paper ballot in any federal recount, which is slow and labor-intensive, and mandates that all federal ballots be printed on recycled paper manufactured in the US — a supply requirement some jurisdictions could not meet immediately and got an escape hatch for.
It hands a federal waiver power to the CISA Director, who could suspend most new device requirements for individual machines for up to two years, a potential soft spot in the mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Paper ballots, no internet connectivity, and risk-limiting audits are the measures election-integrity experts generally treat as the baseline for a verifiable election, and the bill funds most of the compliance it mandates. The real costs are the multi-billion-dollar authorization, the strain on states racing toward a 2020 deadline, and a genuine disruption for the voting-machine industry — which is the point of the bill, not an accident. The hand-count-in-recounts and recycled-paper provisions add administrative burden for modest gain. On balance the design is reasonable, though the 2020 deadline was ambitious.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on July 23, 2019, joined by Sen. Ron Wyden; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration that same day.
Sixteen senators cosponsored the bill — 14 Democrats and 2 independents — but no further action of any kind was ever taken.
The Rules Committee, chaired by a Republican, never held a markup or reported the bill, and the bill's action history ends with the referral.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still sitting in committee, so it expired without ever being debated or voted on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Voting machine manufacturers and other proprietary election vendors, who avoided being required to publish their source code, disclose hardware designs, build US-made paper-ballot systems, and disconnect machines from the internet — and the states that would have had to comply with new federal mandates on a 2020 timeline.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voting machine makers and election vendors

for.what_they_did: Joined Klobuchar in introducing the bill.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee (Roy Blunt, chair)
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on July 23, 2019; the committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and its action history ends there.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Did not bring election security legislation to the Senate floor; in 2019 he publicly refused to schedule votes on Senate election security bills, calling one package 'highly partisan.'

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; all 17 senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Democrats or independents, and the Republican-chaired Rules Committee and Republican Senate leadership never moved it.

industries.industry: Voting system manufacturers (Election Systems & Software, Dominion, Hart InterCivic)
industries.note: The bill would upend their proprietary, machine-centric business model: hand-marked paper ballots would become the official record in federal elections, source code would have to be published under a royalty-free open license, hardware designs and supply chains disclosed, machines cut off from the internet and wireless, and all systems US-manufactured and federally certified. Their interest in keeping closed systems runs against voters' ability to verify their own ballots.

Over $1 billion in authorized grants would flow to states to buy security assessments, cyber training, and technical support from 'qualified election infrastructure vendors' — a new pool of public money for the industry, tied to US-ownership, disclosure, and incident-reporting conditions.

industries.industry: Ballot printing and recycled paper manufacturers
industries.note: All federal election ballots would have to be printed in the US on recycled US-made paper, and the Election Assistance Commission would pay states' ballot design and printing costs, creating guaranteed demand.
